identity.product: An open-source, intelligent, multi-engine schema design and management tool, where a coding agent and an architect work on the same live design through MCP, and nothing lands unchecked: a schema designed from scratch, reverse-engineered from a database, converted from one engine to another, its intelligence stored with it. Every database is an engine plugin, and the engines come in families: two full-feature engines, engine_mysql and engine_postgresql, each built once across every version of its database, and every managed service, distribution or compatible database falls into its family as a subset of it (MySQL: Percona Server, Amazon RDS, Cloud SQL, Amazon Aurora, TiDB; PostgreSQL: Amazon RDS, Cloud SQL, Amazon Aurora, AlloyDB, Spanner, CockroachDB), declared as facts and checked, not built again: what looks like a dozen engines is two, by the design of the schema. At the centre stands the database SchemaForge keeps its work in: one PostgreSQL database, schema_forge, in the PostgreSQL 18 bundled with the app, every design rows of it under its UUIDv7, holding the cortex every engine shares and each engine's own tables, each owner in its own namespace, designed before any of it is built and locked so every build falls into it.
identity.purpose: SchemaForge builds two things together: the product, and the method it is built by, in which people and coding agents develop together: a design session fixes the database and writes a task file; one agent builds it in one session; gates and a person's review decide; a build's lesson changes the method. Every contributor works the same way, with their own coding agent, and the method is theirs to improve too. And it is a collaborative learning exercise, in the open: people learn a data product from the inside (database design, engines, conversion, CDC, a schema's intelligence), coding with agents, and spec-driven development, by building one together.
identity.repository: schema/cortex, the cortex: its tables and functions, every engine's plugs; schema/dump/schema_forge.sql, the locked dump of the whole database; engines/<engine>, each engine plugin's package (engines/mysql today): its card (owner.toml), its tables and functions (schema/), its seeds (seeds/), its reader, writer and rows module; tools/sf, what every tool shares (the store in a container, the servers, the plug-in); tools/cortex and tools/<engine>, the tools that prove each (tools/cortex/all.py, tools/mysql/all.py); tools/local, the installer, its test and the lock; tools/check.py, the one command every change passes; tools/objectives.py, the objectives' state checked against the issues; specs/, this spec; docs/, the designs, as XML, and docs/pages, the site built from the repository (tools/build_site.py).
identity.specs: root.xml, this file; rules.xml, the rules; brief.xml, every word of the brief coding agents read first (site/agents.xml) and of the Contribute page; guides/, an instruction per kind of contribution (a new engine); rendered with this root and the rules; tasks/, one XML file per task, named by its key once its GitHub issue exists (SF-<issue number>.xml) and by its sequence id and name before (t01-spec-check.xml); lessons.xml, what each build taught, added to and never edited.
identity.branches: Each build: one branch cut from the head of main, one pull request into main, reviewed and merged by the operator. A build reads nothing of an unmerged branch.
identity.issues: One GitHub issue per task; its number keys the task file, the branch, every commit and the PR: SF-<issue number>. A task file is named by its number and a short description, its name: specs/tasks/SF-<issue number>-<name, spaces as hyphens>.xml (specs/tasks/SF-93-spec-check.xml), and specs/tasks/<id>-<name, spaces as hyphens>.xml while the task has no issue. Every task of the sequence has a title, what it delivers in at most 80 characters; its issue is titled `<id> · <name>: <title>` (t01 · spec check: every spec file and owner folder checked, and loaded on PostgreSQL 18), its name as the sequence writes it, and its body is written from its task file.

authority.note: The files that decide. A task reads them by what its file names; what they say is the contract. Nothing a file declares is restated in a spec or worked out at run time. Every quote in a spec is its file's own sentence, verbatim; the spec check refuses a quote its file does not hold.

file.decides: every table of the namespace cortex, in the one database schema_forge, in owner.toml's order: the plugs (plugins, plugin_tables, engines, engine_versions, engine_flavors, object_kinds, schema_migrations), designs and their history (designs, branches, turns, operations, row_changes, locked_versions), and the model every engine shares (namespaces, objects, columns, indexes, index_parts, constraints, constraint_columns, dependencies); one CREATE TABLE statement per file, named after its table, every column commented on its line (the installer makes those its comments in the database); functions/, the log's writer, the turn bell, the checks every engine shares, plugging in, and undo
file.quote: a UUIDv7 made with its row, kept when the name changes

file.decides: an engine plugin's own tables, in the namespace engine_<engine> (engine_mysql.tables), each a plug: its design, UNIQUE (design, id), and the foreign key to the cortex row it extends; functions/, its own checks (engine_mysql.check_flavor)

what an engine plugin declares to the cortex when it is plugged in: the engine, its versions, its flavors with what each refuses and the documentation each fact is from, its kinds of object with their versions and tables, and its tables as plugs
the whole database as CI builds and tests it, every grant and policy among it: what the installer must install, exactly (tools/local/lock.py)
the shape of every owner's folder (an engine's, a feature's, and the cortex's alike): its owner.toml card, the shapes of a table, its seeds/ and migrations/, a rename in two versions

code.decides: engine_mysql: its reader (a live server into the model), rows module (the model as the cortex's and engine_mysql's rows, and back) and writer (the model as SQL)

authority.code: Read first. What the code does is what is merged, never what a spec says about it.

code.decides: every check, each a tool: tools/check.py, tools/cortex/all.py, tools/mysql/all.py, tools/local/install.py and its test, tools/local/lock.py, tools/objectives.py

doc.decides: the earlier plugin design; where it and decision service-plugins differ, the decision decides
connections: what an engine declares, profiles without secrets, the five test steps

authority.not_sources: Earlier branches and their pull requests (#90, #91 among them), the prototype tag, conversations, the README files, the agent files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md: they only point to the brief), every file of docs/ but docs/engines.xml and docs/connections.xml, any page, any document outside the repository.

method.note: How a task is done. Every step binds every task; a task file never loosens one.
method.read: A build starts at its task file (rules.xml kickoff), whose start element sends the agent here. Then, in this order: the code merged on main, every file under schema/, engines/ and tools/; this root; rules.xml; the task file; then the files the task file names. Nothing else: nothing authority not_sources names. A session that reads a file out of this order reads again from the first before it writes anything.
method.silence: Everything a task needs is in those files; the agent assumes nothing and works nothing out. When something is missing, or two of them disagree, stop: build nothing around it, push the branch, and hand the operator the PR with exactly which element is silent or which two lines conflict and what was needed. An agent never changes a schema folder, an authority file or a spec file; a task that needs one changed is a stop, and the operator holds a design session. What the agent decides on its own is only what its task file lists under agent-decides.
method.schema: The schema folders are the database. A table, a column, a type, a constraint, a key, a comment or a rule exists because its file says so, and no code creates, alters or drops one any other way. Version 1 of an owner (cortex, workspace, an engine, a feature) creates its namespace, then every table of its folder, in the order of their foreign keys, ties by file name, then (the cortex) enforce_rules.sql, then every view of its rules folder by file name, then cortex.enforce_rules(<its namespace>), then its seeds/ by file name (rows inserted only where their key is missing), then cortex.grant_roles(<its namespace>) (the workspace: its grants.sql); every version runs as sf_owner (decision database-roles); a later version is a migration file <folder>/migrations/<version>_<name>.sql written in a design session together with the change to the table files, additive as the decision additive-migrations says, a column it adds written last in its table file; the session that writes an owner's version 2 first freezes version 1 as <folder>/migrations/1_tables.sql, its table files and rules exactly as shipped, so the table files always show the newest shape, and applying every version of an owner to an empty database gives exactly its files. No build writes either.
method.session: A build session runs under the operator's build configuration, kept by the operator outside the repository: it denies the tools that spawn, run or message another agent, and turns attribution off. The operator starts it; the agent never changes it.
method.agent: One session, one agent, sequential: the agent that holds the task does every step itself: reading, writing, testing, running the gates, writing the PR. It never spawns, delegates to or messages another agent, subagent or session, and never asks another model to build or verify a part.
method.build: A version of a task file is open to every contributor: each builds it with one agent, on one branch from the head of main, as one PR into main, and any number may build the same version at once. The operator reviews them side by side, merges the best, closes the others unmerged, and adds to lessons.xml what their differences teach (a task file two good builds read differently is a task file to write again). A task once merged carries built, its PR's number, in the sequence; a task is wanted when its file is written and every task its depends names is built. A task is built once what its before element names is merged on main.
method.branch: SF-<issue>-<name>-v<file version>-<model>-<effort>, cut from the head of main: the task's key, its name as its file gives it with spaces as hyphens, the task file's version attribute, and the label the agent writes at kickoff. The task file's start element writes it out.
method.model: The label is <model>-<effort>: the model's own name and the effort it runs at, as its session reports them, lowercase, dots and spaces as hyphens. When the session does not report its effort, the agent asks the operator before it cuts the branch, and is told nothing else.
method.commits: Every commit message starts with the task's key (SF-<issue>). No attribution trailer of any kind, no co-author line, no generated-by line, in a commit or in the PR. Small commits, each leaving tools/check.py green.
method.tests: Tests are Rust tests in the crate the task builds, run by cargo test. A task file's tests element lists every rule its steps state, one item each; the agent writes one test per item and none outside the list: a rule the list lacks is a stop, not a test. A test is named by every word of its item: the item's text lowercased, every run of characters other than a to z and 0 to 9 written as one underscore, none at either end. A test proves one rule on fixtures of its own; it reaches no network and no service, but where its item names Docker, and it writes nothing outside its own temporary folder; it reads files of the repository only as its tests element's how names them. Every test of shared code (the store, the registry, the server, the canvas) runs on every engine of schema_forge_engines::for_tests, and what each engine is tested on is data, never named in test code.
method.gates: Run the task's gates in their order; each is a command and an expectation that is a relation over what the command prints, never a number written down. A gate of kind local runs in the checkout; a gate of kind docker runs against a database in Docker: MySQL, the images and versions engines/mysql/tests/live.rs names; PostgreSQL, the image postgres/manifest.toml's [check] image names by its digest, until the task postgres ships the project's own programs; a gate of kind ci is a workflow of .github/workflows run by GitHub on the PR's head, read with gh run view. A gate that fails is a stop. Every gate's command, exit and matched lines go into the PR.
method.ownership: Create, modify and touch only the paths the task file lists under owns; never open for writing a path it lists under forbid; touch no path it does not list. A PR that touches another path is closed.
method.pr: When every gate is green, or when the build stops (method silence), the agent pushes the branch and opens the PR into main with gh pr create, titled "SF-<issue> <name> v<file version> · <model>-<effort>". Its body, in this order: the root's version and the task file's version; the model label; the session the build ran in, the order the files were read, the account it acted as, and the head of main the branch was cut from; the gate table (gate, command, exit, the lines matched); what stopped, if anything; the hand-off notes, three lists, each entry naming its element, an empty list written none: every sentence where more than one reading came to mind, the reading taken and the line that decides it; every check the agent made beyond its tests, and what it found; anything it worked out from the merged code because no file states it; and, for every step of the task file, the function or test that carries it. The operator reviews and merges; the agent never merges.
method.deliverable: A task delivers code, tests and its PR. Nothing else: no change to a schema folder, an authority file or a spec file.
method.rerun: A task is re-run when its file changes: a new file version and a new branch beside the earlier one; the earlier branch is never amended, and one not merged is closed unmerged.

sequence.note: The objectives, in order (decision engine-order). Each is one issue with its ETA, one branch and one PR, merged by the owner before the next starts (decision branch-per-plugin); what each makes and tests is written on its issue. state is done (its issue closed, its pull requests merged), open, or next; prs names the pull requests that delivered it. tools/objectives.py compares state with the issues on GitHub, so it cannot go stale unseen.

decisions.note: What was decided, when, and where it now lives; what is still open. A confirmed decision is written into the file it names, which is the authority. An open decision is a question no agent answers: it closes, in a design session, before the task it names in closes-before, and the spec check refuses that task's file while it is open.
decisions.decision: The store is PostgreSQL 18, bundled: each platform's release carries its PostgreSQL programs, pinned and covered by the release's checksums, and the app runs them itself. It replaces SQLite (decided earlier the same day) because the schema's rules, types and namespaces are the database's own work in PostgreSQL.

The model is stored relationally: one row per part, every column typed, constrained and documented, in its line and in the database's own comments. JSON holds only what is a value of many columns or a list the engine gives as one: the log's row changes, before and after, a trigger's events, an engine's privileges and options as the server writes them.

One database, schema_forge, installed once, and in it one PostgreSQL schema per owner: cortex (the workspace's tables among it, named workspace_*), ui, and engine_<engine> for each engine (engine_mysql is MySQL's), a feature's beside them. Every design people work on is rows of those tables, keyed by its id in cortex.designs: making a design adds a row, reading a table into one adds its rows, and nothing ever creates a database, a schema or a table for a design. Names and places are unique within a design, never across designs. Every table of a design (all but cortex.designs, the engines' declarations, schema_migrations and the workspace's tables) carries its design in a column design, with UNIQUE (design, id); its primary key stays the one column id. Every reference within a design is FOREIGN KEY (design, column) to (design, id), each with an index on (design, column): no row can point into another design, and reading, changing or deleting one design reads that design's rows only, however many the database holds. The spec check refuses a table of a design without them.

Each owner's tables are in its own namespace: the core owners cortex, ui and workspace, engine_<engine> for each engine, and a feature's (usage). A table is named for what it holds (constraints, dependencies, layout_pins), and an engine's table for the cortex table it extends (engine_mysql.tables, engine_mysql.columns) or for what only it has (engine_postgresql.policies).

A rule a foreign key cannot state is a view of the rows breaking it; cortex.enforce_rules puts a deferred constraint trigger on every table the view reads, so the database refuses at commit any write that breaks it, whoever wrote it; the view is read once per commit, again only after a later write. Every rule is on ice (2026-11-26): the views wait in lab/on-ice/rules, and no owner installs one until the rules are their own owner and schema (decision rules-tables), checked per design.

decision.where: the cortex and every plugin's schema; objective #139

decisions.decision: Every id of every table is a UUIDv7 made with its row (DEFAULT uuidv7(): PostgreSQL 18's own, on 15 to 17 the schema's function of the same name making the same layout), stable on rename and never made from a name; every reference is a UUIDv7, held as FOREIGN KEY (design, column) REFERENCES (design, id) and indexed. There is no BIGINT id and no id counter anywhere: in the cortex, in an engine plugin or in a managed-service plugin. It replaces the decisions id-counters and model-ids, and the BIGINT ids main held until 2026-11-27.

A place in a list people order (namespaces, objects, verbatim statements, required extensions) is a NUMERIC order key, unique in its list: a part put between two takes their midpoint, so nothing is renumbered. A place the server's catalog gives (a column's, an index's, an index part's, a parameter's, a partition's) is an INTEGER position from 1, the server's own order: information_schema does not always give it (MySQL sorts STATISTICS by name), so the reader takes it from SHOW CREATE.

An object's kind is one its engine declares in object_kinds, and nothing else is accepted; what an object holds suits its kind: a routine is a procedure or a function, a view's query is a view's, an engine's table options are a table's. The rule parts-of-their-kind, the cortex's and each engine's, refuses any other at commit, once the rules return (decision rules-tables).
Each design is a row of cortex.designs, its id a UUIDv7 issued when it is made and never changed; everything names the design by it, never by its name, so a rename changes one value.

decision.where: schema/cortex/branches.sql; turns.sql; operations.sql; row_changes.sql; savepoints.sql; locked_versions.sql

decisions.decision: Every change is part of an operation of a turn, appended to the log and never edited; the design is written in the same transaction; the log records every row an operation changed with its values before and after, so its inverse is worked out: undo applies it backwards, redo forwards. Turns form a tree, each following its parent: a branch is a line of turns; switching branch moves the design back to the common turn and forward on the other line; opening a savepoint or a version is that move inside a transaction rolled back; a restore is a new turn of inverses, so nothing is ever lost. Every reference is DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, so the log can put rows back in any order. Proven on production schemas: 450 turns, every state hash-exact (lab/repo_versioning_test.py).
Replaced by uuidv7-everywhere: a part's id is a UUIDv7 made with its row; a part an engine extends keeps the cortex part's id.

The log, the turns and the locked versions are keyed by UUIDv7, issued by the database (uuidv7(), PostgreSQL 18, monotonic within a session), so an id's order is the order it was issued; the decision many-writers says how writers share a database.
Every change belongs to a turn: the agent's, a person's edit, an import; undo works on a whole turn.
A rejected turn is kept, marked rejected, and taken back by a new turn that applies its inverses; nothing is deleted from the log.

The cortex is thin: it holds only what every engine shares and what the canvas and the agent read: designs, branches and history (turns, operations, row changes, savepoints, locked versions), the workspace and the reads people chose, engine versions and kinds of object, and the common model (namespaces, objects, columns, indexes, index parts, keys and their columns, dependencies, tags, verbatim statements). Everything only one engine has (routines, triggers, views, sequences, domains, enums, partitions, extensions, accounts, roles, privileges and every object of its own) is that engine's plugin's, in its namespace engine_<engine>, as typed columns with CHECKs and foreign keys (decision typed-core), in the same database as the cortex rows they refer to, so the database enforces every reference; a row of an engine's table extends one cortex row of the right kind. There is no JSON options column and no table of declarations. A table is held as facts only and its statement written from them, exactly as the server writes it; a program keeps its body as the server holds it. Each plugin proves this in containers of every version it supports before it is merged.

The engine families. Two full-feature engines are built, each once, across every version of its database: engine_mysql (MySQL 5.7, 8.0, 8.4, 9.7) and engine_postgresql (PostgreSQL 15 to 18). The plain engine has the most features; every managed service, distribution and compatible database is a subset of it, a flavor of its plugin, in its schema: MySQL's Percona Server, Amazon RDS, Cloud SQL, Amazon Aurora and TiDB; PostgreSQL's Amazon RDS, Cloud SQL, Amazon Aurora, AlloyDB, Spanner and CockroachDB. A design names its engine, version and flavor. What a flavor refuses (versions, kinds, storage engines, privileges, options, names) is a fact of cortex.engine_flavors, each with the provider's documentation page, refused as the design is written; what it adds follows one rule: a new kind of object is a typed table (TiDB's sequences and placement policies, Percona's compression dictionaries); an option of an existing object is a key of that row's flavor_options JSONB, declared by the flavor and checked; a key that references an object or that two flavors share becomes a typed column. So a subset costs facts and a handful of tables, never a new engine: the full-feature engine is the schema of its whole family. A fork that diverges beyond a subset (MariaDB) becomes an engine of its own, built from its family's engine as a template by the same rule. The two families share the cortex and its principles and nothing else: PostgreSQL's engine is its own, far larger design, never jammed into MySQL's.

The cortex and each plugin are built on their own branch from main and merged by the owner before the next starts. Each has an issue with its number, its ETA, what is made and what is tested; it is done only when its proofs pass in CI on its PR and the owner closes the issue, never on the agent's word. An objective that will miss its ETA says so on its issue with a new time before the ETA passes.

Every line of code main held (the Rust crates, the engines, the schema folders, the lab, the tools) was removed on 2026-11-27, keeping only the spec: specs/, docs/, the site and the README. The objectives rebuild it in order (decision engine-order); a decision whose where names a removed file names what its objective rebuilds.
The cortex, the workspace and each engine version their tables on their own; a database records each owner's applied versions with their checksums.

A feature that needs tables (insight, a semantic layer, design rules, pipelines) is an owner, as an engine is: its own folder (features/<feature>/schema), its own namespace, its own versions and its own rules, and it declares the cortex version it needs. A feature extends the schema by adding its namespace; it never changes the cortex's tables, and the cortex never names a feature's.

A schema changes by versions that add: a table, a column that may be null or has a default, a rule, an index. A rename or a removal takes two versions: the first adds the new and moves the data in the same transaction, a later one removes the old, so a build meets only databases it can read. Every release proves, for every version shipped before, that a database made at that version upgrades to the current one and reads back the same; a namespace whose rows are worked out from the model (insight) may instead be dropped and rebuilt.

Nothing a person may want changed is written in code: the product's name, labels, limits, defaults and the like are rows of cortex.workspace_parameters, a key and a JSON value each, shipped as seeds inserted only where the key is missing, so a value a person changed is never overwritten.

Every written task is open to every contributor's agent at once: everyone who wants to submits a build, and the operator picks the best and merges it. The task file is the whole contract, so builds are compared on it; where they differ, the task file is what to improve. What is wanted is advertised from the sequence: the tasks ready to build, the tasks queued behind them, and the open decisions waiting for a design session.

Everything is XML, written once: the root, the rules, the brief, the guides, the task files and the design (docs/*.xml, the owner template's README.xml, every engine's README.xml). Agents read the XML as it is; the site renders each doc as a page for people (docs/pages/docs.py), so a doc never has a second copy to drift from. Markdown is kept only where a tool looks for it by name: README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md for GitHub, which link to the site, and AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md, which only point an agent to the brief; llms.txt indexes it. tools/check.py refuses any other Markdown file, and any spec or doc that names one.

The tool keeps what it shows and what people keep of it (subject areas and where each object is placed, custom perspectives, layout pins, pinned notes) in a core owner of its own, ui, in every schema's database beside the cortex: apart for clarity, treated as the cortex is. Every change to it is an operation of a turn, versioned by the same log and undone with the design; a row of it that belongs to a part of the design goes when that part goes, and comes back when it is undone (lab/repo_versioning_test.py). Its layouts are worked out afresh every time, so every engine, person and agent sees the same picture; the live selection and the view on screen belong to a session, never stored.

The build order, one objective at a time, each its own issue with an ETA, its own branch and its own PR, merged before the next starts: (1) the spec and README (#138); (2) the thin cortex (#139); (3) the MySQL plugin: MySQL 5.7, 8.0, 8.4 and 9.7, and its subsets Percona Server for MySQL, Cloud SQL for MySQL, Amazon RDS for MySQL and Amazon Aurora MySQL (#140); then the app, a complete product on its first engine (revised by the owner on 2026-11-27): (4) the store and core in Rust (#155); (5) the Engine trait and engine_mysql in Rust, the Python kept as its oracle (#156); (6) the server, the MCP and the read-only query layer on Apache DataFusion (#157); (7) the ui schema, plugged in like any plugin, and the React and TypeScript canvas (#158); (8) editing on the canvas (#159); then, each a plugin like any other that the app takes with no change to core or UI: (9) the PostgreSQL plugin: PostgreSQL 15 to 18, and its subsets Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and AlloyDB (#141); (10) Spanner (#145); (11) CockroachDB (#146). Apache Iceberg, BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse and others come after them. (PostgreSQL as an engine, the database people design for, is not the PostgreSQL the store bundles for its own work.)

Every namespace has its two roles, named after it (consistent naming): <namespace>_owner owns it, runs its migrations and never signs in; <namespace>_service is its service account. The cortex's: cortex_owner; cortex_service, the app, which writes designs, branches and the model, opens and ends turns and locks versions; cortex_agent, the coding agent, the same but reading designs, branches and locked versions only; cortex_reader, reading only. Each plugin's: engine_mysql_owner and engine_mysql_service, engine_postgresql_owner and engine_postgresql_service, and so on. A plugin's owner may reference the cortex tables its own extend and nothing else of the cortex; it cannot touch the cortex or another plugin. No account but an owner can create, alter or drop anything; nobody rewrites the log (cortex.row_changes is written only by cortex.log_row). Every login's password is strong, random and written only to the accounts file. tools/cortex/privileges.py proves every account's grants on every table and function, and each refusal.

A plugin's service account is the only writer of its namespace: no cross-engine writes. The app and the agent write operations of the cortex model alone and read the plugin's tables; an operation that touches anything only the engine knows is written whole by the plugin, as its own account, in the turn the app or the agent opened (decision plugin-operations). Row-level security fences each plugin's service account to its own engine's designs, in the cortex and in its namespace; another engine's account cannot even read it.

A plugin is one package (engines/<engine>: its card, its tables and functions, its seeds, its migrations, its reader and writer, and the tools that vet it) plugged in by one tool in five steps, each as its role: the superuser makes its two roles and its schema, owned by its owner; cortex_owner adds its row and opens the cortex to it (cortex.open_to); its owner makes its tables and lets cortex_owner see them; cortex_owner loads its seeds (engine, versions, flavors, kinds, plugin_tables) and checks every table is a plug (cortex.plug_in); its owner gives the grants, attaches history and puts on the fence (cortex.fit_plugin), since only a table's owner may. A fork (TiDB, MariaDB) is an engine of its own, built from its family's engine as a template, with additions by the rule: a new kind of object is a typed table; an option of an existing object only a flavor has is a key of flavor_options JSONB, declared by the flavor; a key that references an object or that two flavors share becomes a typed column. The families: MySQL (engine_mysql with RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora, Percona, TiDB) and PostgreSQL (engine_postgresql with RDS, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Spanner, CockroachDB), each on the same baseline and principles, never jammed together.

The design is locked three ways: specs/lock.xml holds the SHA-256 of every file of every owner's folder, every owner's card, the owner template and postgres/manifest.toml, written only in a design session, and tools/check.py refuses any locked file that differs from it: this catches drift, a file changed without a design session, not a change made on purpose with its lock rewritten; that is caught by .github/CODEOWNERS, which names the operator for those paths and specs/, main requiring the code owner's review; and at run time by the database roles (database-roles), and by rules no writer can skip, their marks kept where only sf_owner writes.

What PostgreSQL itself holds once the locked design is loaded is kept beside the design: schema/dump/<database>.sql, the schema-only pg_dump of every database the design makes (workspace: the workspace's; <engine>: a schema's, the cortex and that engine), loaded on the image postgres/manifest.toml's [check] image names, versions and pg_dump's restrict key left out. A design session writes the dumps with the lock (tools/schema_dump.py --write), and they are locked like the owners' folders. tools/check.py compares the database the design gives with them on every change, and CI runs tools/check.py on main every day as well, so a database that comes out other than the design was locked fails, naming the file and the lines that differ; the spec check (t01) takes the comparison over. The store (t07) compares each live database with the same dumps when it opens it and every day while it runs, and reports a difference as drift, never repairing it on its own.

Every engine's first feature is a schema opened from a saved connection and filled from the database's own catalogs: its structure from the catalog (MySQL: information_schema, with each object's DDL from SHOW CREATE, read by the dump reader), read only, as one import turn; what the server measures comes in 2.0 (decision definitions-first). Reading a dump file is the feature after it. Every engine follows the same order with its own catalogs.

SchemaForge 1.0 captures the objects and their definitions, and nothing else: every object the engine reads, its definition exactly as the server holds it, and what the definition does not say but the catalog does (a view's definer and security, a routine's characteristics, a trigger's order, an event's schedule), read by the choice of kinds and objects (decision read-scope); the 1.0 schema holds exactly that. 2.0 gathers what goes beyond the design and shapes the designs to come, each part its own owner with its own namespace and versions beside the cortex, never a change to 1.0's tables: the objects' metadata (sizes, estimates, statistics, storage); their usage (per table, per index, per statement, lock waits; decision usage-apart, its tables on ice in lab/on-ice/usage); the server's own (settings, status, capabilities, replication, accounts and connections, privileges per object, instrumentation); and the links between objects, derived (decision insight-layer). 1.0 keeps 2.0 in mind: catalog_sources names each source's part (definition now; metadata, usage and server for 2.0), a read's choice is rows its parts can join, and a read (cortex.source_reads) is what each 2.0 snapshot will hang from. 2.0's design starts from what reading everything costs: a person may choose everything, so every part is bounded by parameters, never code (how far back a server's history is taken, how many statements, how many snapshots kept, how often one is taken), a snapshot keeps the server's counters as it gives them and what changed since the last is worked out, never imported whole, and the read's time limit (gentle-read) bounds it all.

The MySQL engine supports 5.7 (added by task mysql live, t05), 8.0, 8.4 and 9.7, and Percona Server for MySQL 5.7, 8.0 and 8.4 as a flavor of it (decision service-plugins), each read live and tested against its own server; 5.7 is asked the 5.7 way (its catalog, its grants), never through what only 8.0 has.

What each version of an engine's database has and lacks, and what its live read asks of it with the grant each needs, is data: cortex.engine_versions, cortex.engine_features and cortex.catalog_sources, written into schema_forge by the app from the engine's declaration, which stays the one source: no seed holds them, and a database just installed has none until the app first starts. So a person or the agent can ask what a schema may use at its version, what changes when it moves to another, and what a missing grant leaves unread.

2.0's, on ice in lab/on-ice/usage since 2026-11-26 (decision definitions-first); as decided for it: a design is read from a saved connection (cortex.workspace_design_connections), each read recorded in cortex.source_reads. When the server keeps usage (MySQL: performance_schema), it is taken on every read, as the server gives it, sample statements included: the read runs inside the source's own network as its read-only service account. Usage is kept in the feature owner usage (snapshots, object_usage, index_usage, query_digests), each row with the server's own row as it gave it; it is measured, not designed, so it is appended, never changed and never part of a turn, and the design's log stays the design.

A live read asks for the server's version first and reads only what that version has (cortex.catalog_sources). It never hammers or locks up the source: one connection and one statement at a time, one database at a time by its name; a read-only session that gives way (a short lock wait timeout, a time limit on every statement); nothing that touches or counts the data, forces statistics, or changes a setting; only the rows of the database read; and a time limit for the whole read, a parameter, after which it keeps what it read and says what it did not.

While a schema is read from its connection, the canvas shows the read as a train of meshing gears that turns while it runs, one gear per step of the read, the current step's gear lit, finished ones marked done, a step the choice leaves out or the server cannot answer shown skipped with why. Beside it, in words people understand: what is being gathered now and why, the statement sent, what came back, and the statements sent so far, the time taken and the gentle-read limits in force. The steps are the engine's, as it declares them for the server's version, so the screen names no database; every count and statement is the real read's. docs/prototypes/read-screen.html is the prototype, its numbers from the probe of MySQL 5.7, 8.0, 8.4 and 9.7.

decision.where: schema/cortex/read_scopes.sql; schema/cortex/read_scope_kinds.sql; schema/cortex/read_scope_objects.sql; schema/cortex/workspace_design_connections.sql; schema/cortex/source_reads.sql; docs/live-mysql.xml; the read screen

decisions.decision: Once connected, the person chooses what a design takes from its database, and the first choice is simple: everything (every object the engine reads at the server's version, with its definition), or choose. Choosing opens two finer choices, each set to all until changed: the kinds of object, as the engine declares them for the server's version (tables, views, procedures, functions, triggers, events); and the objects, picked from the list or by a name or a pattern. A choice is typed rows, never JSON: cortex.read_scopes (everything, or not), cortex.read_scope_kinds and cortex.read_scope_objects; it is never changed, a new choice is a new row. The design's connection names its newest (cortex.workspace_design_connections.scope), so a later read asks the same, and each read names the one it ran with (cortex.source_reads.scope); the read screen runs only the steps the choice needs. The parts beyond definitions (metadata, usage, the server's own) are 2.0's choices, made the same way (decision definitions-first).

Every option an engine names is a typed column of the table that extends the part it belongs to, written only where the statement writes it; the engine's reader refuses an option its tables have no column for, so a new release's option is a new column in a design session, never a row of text. There is no table of keys and values: keys an engine leaves to its users to name (Iceberg's table properties) are one JSONB column. Which version has which option is data (decision version-facts), never a column.

A build may run in any session the operator chooses: a new one, one that holds other work, or another agent's. What makes it a build is that it works from the spec alone: it reads the files whole, in the method's order, before it writes anything, and takes nothing said in the session or remembered from other work as authority; what the files do not say is a stop. So a task file gives the same result wherever it is built, here or by another agent; two builds that differ show where the task file is unclear, and a design session writes it again.

The service accounts are the database's (database-roles): every version of a namespace runs as its <namespace>_owner, the app as cortex_service and each plugin as its <namespace>_service, never as a person's login. A service account is never a GitHub identity: a build is pushed and its pull request opened under the GitHub account of whoever runs it, and the code owner reviews and merges.
The schema is designed first and locked: no build creates or changes a table; a change is a design session's migration and table files.
The spec check is Rust, in tools/specs, run by cargo test and tools/check.py.
Tasks are keyed SF-<GitHub issue number>; a task file's name is its key and its name (SF-93-spec-check.xml).

Pull requests #90 and #91 are held, unmerged; what they built is built again from the sequence: the registry in t03; the engine's word for a namespace, a connection's summary, the API contract and the server in t09; the canvas and its browser tests in t10.
The operation kinds (add_table, rename_column and the rest), what each changes and how the agent calls it.

An agent's change enters the current model as it is made, and its turn commits when the agent ends it, so every open canvas shows it through the bell and the design is never held waiting for a verdict. The verdict comes after: keeping it needs nothing; rejecting it is cortex.undo of that committed turn, itself a turn that can be undone. There is no staging copy of the model.

An operation is one transaction on one connection, so it lands whole or not at all. An operation that touches any engine row is written entirely by that engine's plugin, as its service account: the operation's row, the cortex model rows and its own namespace's rows, fenced by row-level security to its engine's designs (the grants plug_in already gives it). An operation of the shared model alone (a rename on the canvas) is written by the app or the agent. The app's account (cortex_service) and the agent's (cortex_agent) open, commit and reject turns, as plug_in grants them; a plugin's never does, it only adds its operations to a turn one of them opened. No transaction spans two accounts.

The store sets schema_forge.operation with set_config(..., true), for the operation's transaction alone, never for the session, so a pooled connection cannot carry it into another caller's work. Every write runs SERIALIZABLE (decision many-writers) and is retried on a serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001) or deadlock (40P01) with bounded, jittered backoff; any other refusal comes back to the caller as a typed error naming its SQLSTATE.

A design has at most one open turn, held by the database (a unique index on the design of open turns), not by the app: a second writer, a person on the canvas or an agent over the MCP, is told who holds the design and since when, and waits or tries again. Undo stays exact because no two turns interleave.

The bell is LISTEN schema_forge_turns on one connection of its own, outside the pool. A notification is not durable, so the listener remembers the last commit number it saw per design; after every reconnect it listens again and reads every turn committed past it, and so does a reader that sees a gap in the numbers. A canvas that falls behind the server's broadcast is told to reload its design.

Coding agents reach the MCP over stdio: schema-forge mcp runs as the agent's child process and signs in as cortex_agent, with no network port to guard. A stdio server shares the agent's trust domain, so it reads only cortex_agent's credential, never the whole accounts file (MCP's local server security guidance). Streamable HTTP comes later, behind a flag and a token. schema-forge serve listens on 127.0.0.1 unless told otherwise.

The fence of row-level security is one uncorrelated subquery, the designs of the asking account (design IN (SELECT cortex.designs_of(current_user))), worked out once per statement on the indexed design column, not a function called for every row: the commonest cost of row-level security, found in the research for the architecture page. tools/cortex/privileges.py proves the fence unchanged; a test proves the plan evaluates it once.

An undo's operation records the turn it undid (cortex.operations.undoes). After every undo the cortex marks each turn of the design by whether its changes are in the model: undone when an undo in effect undid it, committed otherwise, worked out newest first, since an undo always undoes an older turn. So undoing an undo is a redo, and undoing a restore brings back exactly what it undid, the undos among it included; restore is undoing, newest first, every turn after the one wanted that is still in effect. Found while building the store: marking only the turn undone left a turn marked committed whose changes were gone. tools/cortex/history.py and the store's tests prove it by the model's hash.

Python is for tests and prototypes; Rust is production. Everything SchemaForge ships and runs (the store and core, every engine's reader, rows and writer, the server, the MCP, the query layer) is Rust, in the workspace. Python stays for the tools that build, prove and check it (containers, round trips, the site, the spec checks) and for a prototype that proves a design before its Rust is written; a Python prototype is deleted once the Rust equals it (decision python-engine-retired).

The Python engine_mysql (engines/mysql/reader.py, rows.py, writer.py) was the prototype that proved the schema; the Rust engine is the real one. #156 ports it to Rust and proves the Rust reader, rows and writer give the Python's rows exactly on every server; then, in the same objective, the tools that use it (tools/mysql/roundtrip.py, flavors.py, show.py and tools/local/qa.py) call the schema-forge binary instead, and the Python engine is deleted. From then on the Rust round trips are the reference. The Python tools that run containers and checks stay.

The canvas is held to a measured speed, on the largest real schema there is, the owner's private production schema of 2,608 objects (never committed; run locally, as the private MySQL proofs are): it opens and draws in under 3 seconds, and panning and zooming keep every frame under 50 ms. A browser test (Playwright) measures both; the 665-object schema and a generated 2,608-object sample, committed, hold CI to the same numbers.

Parked by the owner on 2026-11-27: a one-command start, the schema-forge binary running its own PostgreSQL 18 (decision postgresql-bundled) so a user needs no DBA install, no superuser and no accounts file. Not scheduled; until it is, SchemaForge is installed by a DBA with tools/local/install.py.

Listening on 127.0.0.1 is not an authentication boundary: a web page can reach a local port through the browser (DNS rebinding). serve checks every request's Origin and a token made at each launch, on the API and the websocket, and refuses anything else.

When the MCP is served over HTTP, a schema of its own, mcp, plugged in like ui with mcp_owner and mcp_service, holding only what the cortex has no place for: the clients allowed to connect (token hashes, never tokens; scopes; revocation) and an audit of every tool call, reads and refusals included. Never design data: what an agent changes stays in the cortex's turns, operations and log; sessions stay in the server's memory. Over stdio (decision mcp-stdio) it needs none.

Rust edition 2024 with the toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml (1.94 or later); workspace lints with unsafe_code forbidden and clippy warnings failing the build; cargo-deny for licences and advisories. tokio-postgres 0.7 with deadpool-postgres and rustls (decision pg-driver); mysql_async 0.37; axum 0.8 with tower-http, the canvas embedded in the binary; rmcp pinned to an exact version; Apache DataFusion 55, the query layer alone depending on it and signing in as cortex_reader, so no query can write; engines depend on arrow-schema only; thiserror in the libraries, anyhow in the binary alone; ids are typed (DesignId, TurnId and the rest) and made by the database. The canvas: Vite, React and TypeScript, its diagrams plain SVG laid out by rule; its API types generated from the server's OpenAPI. Tests run against one PostgreSQL 18 container per run that tools/app/all.py makes and installs, each test in a design of its own.

The tables of the rules: their links on the hierarchy, groups, exceptions, packs and findings (docs/rules.xml), as their own owner and namespace in schema_forge; the integrity rules on ice in lab/on-ice/rules return with them, each checking only the designs a commit changed.
The tables of a CDC pipeline between two schemas, by their stable ids.

One PostgreSQL cluster per workspace, its data in the workspace folder (pgdata/), started when the workspace is opened and stopped when it closes; reached only through a Unix socket in that folder, no network port, so only the user who owns the folder connects. How it starts, stops and recovers is the store task's.

The PostgreSQL 18 programs are built by the project's own CI from the official source tarball, its hash pinned, for each platform, and published as the project's release assets; a manifest in the repository pins each platform's asset by SHA-256, and one fetch tool, used by the release, by developers and by tests, refuses anything whose hash differs. The store's tests start a real cluster from those programs. A task before the store builds this.

The store talks to PostgreSQL through tokio-postgres (async), with a connection pool and rustls for TLS, so the same code serves the bundled cluster over its Unix socket and, one day, a central team server over TCP and TLS; only the connection changes.

The store is written for many writers from the start: the database issues the log's ids (uuidv7(), PostgreSQL 18), every write runs SERIALIZABLE so two writers cannot together break a rule each alone keeps, and a PostgreSQL advisory lock takes the place of a lock file.

The app works from memory and the database keeps the record: no click, screen or agent read is a query. Opening a design loads every row of it once, one indexed read per table by its design column, into the app's model; every screen and every read of the design is answered from that model, and a screen is redrawn only where a change touches it. An edit changes the model at once and is committed as one turn, one transaction; if the database refuses it, the model takes it back. The log is the change feed: every turn has a number in its design's commit order (turns.seq), so a copy that holds the design at a number catches up by reading the turns after it, and a gap is always seen. NOTIFY only rings the bell (the design and the number, after commit); it is never the change, since a listener that was away misses it, and on every connect the copy asks the log for what came after its number. Only questions across designs (search, compare, reports, usage history) are sent to the database as queries. A snapshot of a design at a number, replayed from there, and reading PostgreSQL's replication stream for a team's central server come only if a measurement asks for them.

What is worked out about the model, kept apart from it in a feature owner insight, so a person or an agent can search and question a design through the MCP: the links between objects, derived from their bodies, never typed: one row per fact a body states about another object (calls, reads, writes, on, references, creates, drops, alters, foreign key, or unresolved), with the object it names when it resolves, the line and the statement it was read from as evidence, and for a name built while it runs the pattern of its fixed parts, so one fact can name every table it can reach; walked both ways for impact (2.0, decision definitions-first); cards composed mechanically from the model; annotations an agent writes, with the model and the input hash; embeddings (pgvector, HNSW) of cards and annotations, searched together with full-text and exact names and every hit confirmed against the model. Kept fresh from the log: an accepted turn's row_changes name the objects whose rows are redone. Rebuilt, never logged or migrated. The MCP's read tools: search (finds candidates), object (one object whole), impact (the walk), sql (every count and list, as a read-only role). The embedding model is the decision embedding-models. A semantic layer (business terms, measures) is authored, so it is its own owner, logged by turns; its embeddings are insight's.

Embeddings come from either of two kinds of model, chosen per workspace, as the database is: local, a model bundled with the app and run on the machine (works offline, nothing leaves it), or remote, an embedding API or the team server's own model (its key from the environment or the system keychain, never in a profile or a table); on a team server the server embeds, so everyone shares one model and one index. Every embedding row names its model and its dimension; changing the model rebuilds insight's embeddings, nothing else. Which local model and which APIs close with insight-layer.

pgvector is compiled into the project's PostgreSQL 18 build from the first release, its version pinned and covered by the same checksums, so vector search arrives with a feature owner and never with new programs.

What the steward agent may do alone and what stays a person's: which pull requests it may merge (a task's build, a contributor's, a design session's never), what its review must prove beyond the gates, how often it runs and on what, how it records a lesson, how it starts the next build, and how a person stops or overrides it. Until it closes, a person reviews and merges, and no agent merges.

decision.where: sequence o4 to o8; decision engine-order

decisions.decision: The order of the work after the store: the store and core, the engines' interface, the server with the MCP and the query layer, the canvas, then editing (o4 to o8); the insight layer and the rules come after the sequence's eleven objectives.
The server's API over the store: every route and type, written before it is built.
